title: Those who reflect
hookLine: the closing of Al 'Imran, from the night sky to patience (3:190–200)
tomorrow: Jordan: 'wait, Joseph with the coat is in the Qur'an too?'

cards: Finals week has a look: the glow of a laptop at midnight, flashcards on the bed, a cold cup of tea.
Amira has a chemistry final in the morning, and she's started asking the question that comes at that hour: what's any of this for? Dadi taps on the door. "Come outside. Five minutes."
In the yard, Dadi just points up. Clouds moving, a few stars, a plane blinking across. "Subhanallah," she says, and starts to recite.

teach.h: THE PROPHET LOOKED UP AND RECITED.
teach.b: She's reciting the end of Surah Al 'Imran, and these verses have been said under the sky before. Ibn Abbas, as a boy, spent a night in the Prophet's house.
He saw him, peace be upon him, wake in the dark, look up at the sky, and recite these verses.

teach.h: THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.
teach.b: They open in Pickthall's words: in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of night and day, are tokens for people of understanding, "Such as remember Allah, standing, sitting, and reclining," and who look at the sky and say: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain."

Not in vain. That's the first answer to Amira's question. Then the people pray, and the answer comes: "Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost. Ye proceed one from another."
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an answers 'is my effort wasted?' by saying no worker's work is lost, and that we all come from one another.
The flashcards count. So does the night shift, and the knee exercises.
And the passage closes on what to do with that: be patient, outdo others in patience, stand firm, and be mindful of Allah. Steadfast, under a sky that wasn't made in vain.

how: Some Muslims recite the closing verses of Al 'Imran, 3:190–200, on waking for the night prayer, following the Prophet's practice described by Ibn Abbas.

o: people who pray only in the quiet of the night
people who look at creation and remember Allah
scholars who study the stars to set the calendar

games.q: the closing of Al 'Imran — tap the pairs.
p: saw the Prophet look up and recite
Thou createdst not this in vain
what they say to the sky

s: the Qur'an treats looking at the sky as a distraction from worship
it praises those who remember Allah and consider the creation of the heavens and the earth.
Ibn Abbas saw the Prophet wake at night, look at the sky and recite these verses
he spent the night in the Prophet's house as a boy (Sahih al-Bukhari).

games.q: your friend's mom cleans offices overnight. she says her work 'doesn't count for much.' what does 3:195 give you to say?
o: no worker's work, male or female, is lost; we all come from one another.
only religious work, like prayer and fasting, counts before Allah.
work counts once people see it; she should ask for more credit.
games.why: "I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost. Ye proceed one from another."

practice: Go to a window or step outside and look at the sky for the whole sit, day or night. Find one thing up there that you didn't make and can't change: a cloud, a star, the color.
Let your work for today be smaller than it, and still not lost.

wordCard.voice: Those who reflect: the people at the end of Al 'Imran who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying down, and look at the sky.

orig.note: Arabic: people of understanding, those the night sky speaks to in 3:190.

carryVoice: Keep it for the morning: be patient and steadfast; no worker's work is lost. Four passages, read whole.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:190 and 3:200 (tokens for people of understanding; be patient, outdo in patience, stand firm)
